public.title: Seedlings Beyond the Gap
public.incident: Fruit fragments and new seedlings appear beyond a broken stretch of canopy, far from the nearest fruiting parent trees.
public.atmosphere: The pattern forms overnight and links high feeding sites to open regeneration plots.
public.question: Which species is involved, and what process best explains plants crossing the canopy gap?

explanationChoices.label: Mobile seed dispersal
explanationChoices.description: A fruit-feeding animal carries or passes seeds between separated forest patches.

explanationChoices.label: Wind dispersal
explanationChoices.description: Air currents carried the seeds across the opening.

explanationChoices.label: Unrecorded planting
explanationChoices.description: People established seedlings outside the documented restoration plots.

explanationChoices.label: Hidden parent trees
explanationChoices.description: The survey overlooked nearby fruiting trees beneath dense cover.

explanationFeedback.mobile-seed-dispersal: This mechanism connects elevated fruit feeding, overnight movement, and seedlings beyond a canopy break.
explanationFeedback.wind-dispersal: Wind can move some seeds, but the fruit remains and concentrated feeding sites point to an animal vector.
explanationFeedback.human-planting: No planting record or regular spacing supports deliberate restoration at these points.
explanationFeedback.parent-trees-missed: The mapped fruiting trees and genetic sampling place the parent source across the canopy gap.

resolution.headline: A forest connection made on the wing
resolution.diagnosis: Livingstone’s flying fox moved fruit material and seeds between separated canopy patches, supporting regeneration beyond the gap.
evidenceChain: Fruit and flower remains identify an above-ground plant food source.
Roost-centered group movement and wide forelimbs support aerial travel.
The island range and overnight route connect feeding trees to distant seedling plots.
resolution.ecologicalRole: Fruit bats can move seeds and pollen through island forests, helping connect plant populations across fragmented canopy.
resolution.taxonomy: Pteropus livingstonii is a pteropodid fruit bat in the mammal order Chiroptera.
resolution.misconception: Bats are not ecological bystanders at fruiting trees; feeding can transport seeds and pollen beyond the parent plant.
rejectedAlternatives: Wind does not explain the associated fruit pulp and elevated feeding sites.
Unrecorded planting is unsupported by site records and the irregular seedling pattern.
